It found that sweep_expired_offers also runs on every peer registration, so a peer joining mid-file would have destroyed an in-progress transfer through a path my instruction did not mention. It added that test and the offer-keybook in ActiveTransfer. Mutation 3 fails ONLY that test, which is exactly why it was worth adding.
hub_ttl_fix_verified.mutation_design_note: mutations 1 and 2 are equivalent (both disable the continued-check) and fail the same two tests; mutation 3 targets a different code path entirely. The builder ran all three rather than stopping at the two I asked for.

defect_i_found_in_my_own_fix.how: the builder's closing note mentioned exempted offers counting toward caps; following that thread led to the map itself
defect_i_found_in_my_own_fix.attack: one live offer plus unlimited distinct transfer_ids: every pull is authorised, every Delivered insert lands, and each entry lives TRANSFER_MEMORY_MS (30 min). Note Delivered only means the frame reached the source's channel -- it does not mean the source accepted the session, so a source answering busy still leaves an entry behind.
defect_i_found_in_my_own_fix.scale: roughly 80 bytes per entry including table overhead; ~550 pulls/second sustains ~80 MB. MAX_OFFERS_TOTAL bounds offers but nothing bounded transfers.
defect_i_found_in_my_own_fix.fix_dispatched: cap at 4 * MAX_OFFERS_TOTAL, evicted in BATCHES rather than one at a time -- single-entry eviction at the cap would rescan 16k entries on every subsequent pull, converting a memory bound into a CPU one
defect_i_found_in_my_own_fix.fails_closed: a forgotten transfer simply returns to the TTL gate, which is the pre-existing behaviour
